description: Red Path is a team taking on "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map". We're building an interactive map that helps a future Mars astronaut plan a surface excursion in Gale Crater. It layers NASA data (topography, orbital imagery, thermal, spectral and radiation) and calculates a walking route that avoids steep slopes and obstacles. A safety panel shows distance, time, slope and conditions, and a helmet-style HUD view makes it usable in the field.
summary:
Redpath is an EVA planner for Mars built on real data: USGS 1 m terrain, HiRISE imagery and NASA rover waypoints at Gale crater. It makes six inventions, each built and tested:

Certified go or no-go. A separate checker, sharing no code with the planner, re-derives every claim from the raw terrain, and a verdict shows only if it passes. It catches seven planted planner faults, including a real bug from this project.
Return Horizon. A live map of every place the crew can still get back to shelter from, with a reserve.
Rescue Horizon. Where a downed partner can still be carried or driven home in time.
Drift Guard. Margins assume the worst position inside an error circle that grows with distance walked, because Mars has no GPS.
One safety margin. It covers return, rescue, storm and daylight, and names the tightest limit.
Fail-cautious live mode. A stalled position feed widens the error, never narrows it.
It runs offline, which matters because Mars crews can't call Earth for real-time help.
details:
What's new: a plan that proves itself before you trust it. Redpath doesn't show GO or NO-GO until a second, separate program has re-derived every number from the raw terrain. A planner bug can't approve itself, and an unverified plan prints in red as NOT CERTIFIED. Mars crews can't call Earth for real-time help, so a plan has to be checkable on the spot.

Also new: what happens if the other person goes down. Besides the Return Horizon, the Rescue Horizon shows where a downed partner could still be carried or driven home inside their suit limits. Both feed one safety margin with daylight and the storm warning, and it names the limit that is tightest.

How it works. It plans a walk over a 20 m grid built from the USGS 1 m terrain model of Gale crater and tracks the crew's position with a Mars-specific error model. It tells the crew when to turn back. A stalled position feed makes the margins more cautious, never less. It has a 3D terrain view, a helmet display, a plain-language assistant, printable cue sheets and GPX, GeoJSON and CSV export. It works fully offline.

Benefits and intended impact. It turns maps into clear go or no-go decisions with the reasoning visible. The aim is a planning aid that crews and mission planners can inspect and challenge.

Tools.

  • Code: JavaScript (Leaflet, three.js, Web Workers, a service worker), a dependency-free Node.js server, and Python with numpy and Pillow for data extraction.
  • Data: USGS 1 m terrain and 25 cm orthophoto mosaic, NASA MOLA, Viking, THEMIS and CTX imagery, and NASA rover waypoints.
  • Sun model: NASA GISS Mars24 method.
  • Assistant: a hosted NVIDIA language model through a server proxy. It only rewords the planner's own numbers and is checked against them.
  • Development: AI-assisted, using Claude Code.
  • Hardware: none.

Factors considered.

  • No GPS and no real-time link to Earth.
  • Rescue as well as return.
  • Daylight and storms.
  • Honest limits: speeds and thresholds are assumptions, the storm doses are illustrative, there is no oxygen or consumables model, and nothing has been tested with real suits or crews. It is a planning aid, not flight-qualified software.
